name: Recording yourself

lead: Recording yourself means capturing your speech on a phone or microphone and listening back. It is used as a basic feedback step in voice improvement, helping people hear how they come across and adjust.

Playback lets a speaker hear pacing, filler words and tone from the outside, which practitioners say differs from how one hears oneself while talking. That feedback then feeds into practice. No studies were found testing it for changing perceived attractiveness or authority.

paras: People record a short clip of normal speech or a reading, listen back for pace, filler words and tone, then try again. It is often combined with exercises such as reading aloud or slowing down.
No risks are documented in the sources reviewed. Hearing your own recorded voice can feel unfamiliar at first.

chain: Hear and see yourself as others do
angle.text: Recording yourself lets you hear your pacing, filler words and tone as others do, so you can adjust and practice a voice that comes across with more clarity and authority. It works as a feedback step alongside voice exercises.

lead: Recording yourself means capturing audio or video of your own speech and movement so you can review it and adjust. In looksmaxxing circles it is used for voice feedback: hearing how pitch, pace, clarity and filler words sound to others, and then refining them.

Speakers often find their recorded voice sounds different from the voice they hear while talking. Because sound also travels through the skull to the inner ear, which favours lower frequencies, a person's own voice seems deeper and fuller to them than to listeners; a recording captures only the airborne sound [1]. Reviewing recordings gives an outside view that practitioners use alongside rehearsal and feedback from others [2].

paras: People record short speech samples, calls or readings and listen back, noting pace, volume, monotone stretches and filler words. Some also film themselves to review posture and gestures. Public-speaking organisations use evaluation and feedback as a central training method, with members critiquing each other's speeches [2].
The mismatch between how a voice sounds internally and on playback is sometimes called voice confrontation, and arises because bone conduction adds low-frequency resonance that recordings lack [1].
